1-2: Pairs from two groups, such as one hat and one scarf, every hat with every scarf.
Handshakes or phone calls among a few friends, each pair once.
Two-digit numbers written with given digits, with or without a digit used twice.
Lines of children or towers of blocks, with one of them kept in one place or kept out of one.
Routes through a middle stop: the roads of each part of the way multiplied.
Paying a small amount with coins of two or three values, the order of the coins not mattering.
Two-digit numbers whose digits add up to a given number.
A robot's steps, some to the right and one or two up, in any order: how many orders there are.
Cones of two scoops from a few flavours, when the order of the scoops matters and when it does not.
Flags of two or three stripes, neighbouring stripes in different colours.
Two dice or spinners: the ways they can show a given total, the first and the second counted apart.
Each of a few things one of two ways, a coin heads or tails, a lamp on or off: every new thing doubles the results.
Climbing a few stairs one or two steps at a time: the ways sorted by the last step.
The different amounts a few coins make, one or more of them used at a time.
Rows of a few things where some are alike, such as two red beads and a blue one: swapping the alike ones makes no new row.
Four children split into two pairs: the partner of one child decides the whole split.
There and back by different paths: for each path there, every path back but that one.
Two things put in a row of places so that they are not side by side: their places listed in order.
3-4: A knockout tournament: every game sends one player home, so there is one game fewer than there are players.
Numbers that read the same from both ends: the first half of the digits decides the rest.
A few identical sweets shared among three children, each getting at least one: listed by what the first child gets.
People round a table, where turning the table round gives the same seating: one person's seat is fixed first.
In half of all the orders of a few people one stands before another, since swapping those two pairs the orders off.
How many numbers in a range contain a given digit, or how many times a digit is written.
A team with a captain: the members chosen, and then one of them to lead.
Lines where boys and girls take turns: once it is known who stands first, the boys' orders are multiplied by the girls' orders.
Things handed back so that nobody gets their own, hats or letters: listed one by one for three or four people.
The choices a condition rules out, counted and taken from all the choices: two children who are not both girls.
Rectangles made of a given number of square tiles: the pairs of numbers that multiply to it, each pair once.
Pairs whose total is even or odd: counted as odd with odd and even with even, case by case.
Stacks of one or more of a few different books: the stacks of each height counted and then added.
Two things of different kinds bought from three kinds, such as a cup and a saucer: each pair of kinds multiplied, and the products added.
Two rooks of different colours on a small board that do not attack: the second keeps off the first one's row and column.
5-6: Menus and outfits with one combination that is not allowed.
Dominoes and other pairs of numbers, a double counted once.
Two dice: the ways the pair can show a given total.
Round trips: there and back, with and without the same road twice.
Fences and flags of several parts, neighbouring parts in different colours and one end fixed.
Robot paths across a board, some squares blocked.
Numbers with conditions on their digits: all different, odd, or a given digit sum.
Seats in a row with two rules at once, such as sitting together and not at an end.
Teams under conditions: someone must be in, and two refuse to be together.
Rectangles or squares of every size in a small grid of cells.
A round-robin where every player won a different number of games: the wins are 0, 1, 2 and so on, so each order of players is one result.
Numbers chosen so that no pair adding up to a given total is taken whole: each pair gives none, its smaller or its bigger number.
Things chosen from a row so that no two are next to each other: closing up the gaps turns it into a plain choice.
Rows of numbers where each new one is the biggest or the smallest so far: from the back, every place but the first has two choices.
Problems solved by pupils, counted two ways, by the problems and by the pupils: the one count not given follows.
Rows of coloured balls worked back from how many rows there are to how many balls share a colour.
Different things shared so that nobody is left out: all the ways less those in which someone gets nothing.
Numbers paired up so that in every pair the bigger is at least twice the smaller: the small numbers must go with the big ones.
A small table whose rows and columns must add up to multiples of 3: the free cells decide all the others.
Seats on the two sides of a booth with room for so many on a side: the people split between the sides first, then each side seated.
